title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Differential equations help us understand changing environments




For some natural phenomena it can be easier to describe them in terms of derivatives than give an explicit function.

Example
Lotka-Volterra models to describe predator prey dynamics: \[
\begin{align}
\frac{dN_1}{dt}&=r_1N_1\left(\frac{K_1-N_1-\alpha N_2}{K_1}\right)\\
\frac{dN_2}{dt}&=r_2N_2\left(\frac{K_2-N_2-\beta N_1}{K_2}\right)
\end{align}
\]
where \(N_1, N_2\) are the population of prey and preadtor respectively.

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Separation of variables



A first-order ODE of the form \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x)g(y)\) can be solved in the following steps:

Move like terms to the same side, including differentials \(dx\text{ and } dy\). This is a convenient shorthand for more involved calculus steps.
Apply the integral to both sides.
Rearrange equations to isolate in terms of dependent variable.
Use initial conditions (if given) to find \(C\) values.
Evaluate the bounds if definite intervals are given.



✏️ Solve for \(y\) in \(\frac{dy}{dx}=4y\)

\[
\begin{align}
\frac{dy}{4y}& =dx \\
\int\frac{dy}{4y}&=\int dx\\
\frac{1}{4}\ln y&=x+C_1 \\
\ln y&=4x+C_2\\
y&=e^{4x+C_2} \\
y&=e^{C_2}e^{4x} \\
y&=Ce^{4x}
\end{align}
\]

Verify that \[\int \frac{1}{ax+b} dx = \frac{\ln(ax+b)}{a}.\]



An oil spill off the coast of Santa Barbara is spreading rapidly. Previous spills and an analysis of the current data indicate that the oil is spreading at a daily rate of:

\[
\frac{dA}{dt}=-0.001A+60,
\]
where \(A\) is the area of the oil spill in \(km^2\) and \(t\) is the time in days.

Find an equation that models the spread of oil in total area. Hint: exercise 1.
After the first day the oil has spread to 25 \(km^2\). What steps would you take to find when will the oil spill cover all of the Santa Barbara Channel (~5850 \(km^2\))? You don’t need to compute it, just come up with a solid plan.

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Solution 2.a.
We are given the differential equation:
\[
\frac{dA}{dt} = -0.001 A + 60
\]
Step 1: Rearrange for separation of variables
\[
\frac{dA}{dt} = 60 - 0.001 A \quad \implies \quad \frac{dA}{60 - 0.001 A} = dt
\]
Step 2: Integrate both sides
\[\int \frac{1}{60 - 0.001 A} \, dA = \int dt\]
Using the hint:
\[-1000 \ln(60 - 0.001 A) = t + C_1\]
Step 3: Solve for (A)
\[\ln(60 - 0.001 A) = -0.001 (t + C_1)\]
\[60 - 0.001 A = e^{-0.001 (t + C_1)} = C e^{-0.001 t} \quad (\text{combine constants})\]
\[0.001 A = 60 - C e^{-0.001 t}\]
\[\boxed{A(t) = 60000 - C e^{-0.001 t} \text{, \  where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.}}\]

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Limits

Definition
We say a number \(L\) is the limit of a function \(f(x)\) as its variable \(x\) approaches a number \(c\), if the function’s output values \(f(x)\) approach \(L\) when \(x\) get closer to \(c\).

We write this symbolically as:
\[
\large
\lim_{x\to c} f(x)=L
\]

We read this as: “The limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches \(c\) is \(L\).”

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Limits example: numerical

What is the limit of \(f(x)=2x^2-4\) as \(x\) approaches 2?
We need to examine the values of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) gets closer to 2 from both sides.

✏️

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Limits example: numerical

What is the limit of \(f(x)=2x^2-4\) as \(x\) approaches 2?
We need to examine the values of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) gets closer to 2 from both sides.

From both directions it looks like \(f(x)\) converges to 4.
So, we say that “The limit of \(2x^2-4\) as \(x\) approaches 2 is 4”. We can write it like this:

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Rules for differentiation (1)

Constant Rule
Let \(c\) be a constant (so, a number). If \(f(x) = c\), then \(f'(x)=0\). Equivalently
\[\frac{d}{dx}c = 0\]
Power Rule
Let \(n\) be a (real) number, if \(f(x)= x^n\), then \(f'(x) = nx^{n-1}\). Equivalently \[
\frac{d}{dx}[x^n]
=nx^{n-1}.
\]
Examples ✏️
\[
\begin{align}
&y=100 & &f(x)=x^5 & &f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2}
\end{align}
\]

title: Bren Math Workshop

Sum and Difference Rules
✏️

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Rules for differentiation (2)

Sum and Difference Rules
Let \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) be differentiable functions. Then
\[
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dx}[f(x)+g(x)]=\frac{d}{dx}f(x)+\frac{d}{dx}g(x) \\
\frac{d}{dx}[f(x)-g(x)]=\frac{d}{dx}f(x)-\frac{d}{dx}g(x)
\end{align}
\]
😵All this says is: if the function has pieces that are added or subtracted you can take the derivative of each individual piece and add those derivatives.
The \(\frac{d}{dx}\) notation can be a lot here, the prime notation is a bit better:
\[
\begin{align}
[f(x)+g(x)]'=f'(x)+g'(x) \\
[f(x)-g(x)]'=f'(x)-g'(x)
\end{align}
\]
✏️ Example
\[
f(x)=x^3-x^2-15
\]

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Summary of differentiation rules










Differentiation Rule
\(f'(x)\) notation
\(\frac{d}{dx}\) notation




Constant Rule
\(f(x)=c \Rightarrow f'(x)=0\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[c]=0\)


Power Rule
\(f(x)=x^n \Rightarrow f'(x)=n x^{n-1}\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[x^n]=n x^{n-1}\)


Sum Rule
\((g(x)+h(x))'=g'(x)+h'(x)\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[g(x)+h(x)]=\frac{d}{dx}g(x)+\frac{d}{dx}h(x)\)


Difference Rule
\((g(x)-h(x))' = g'(x)-h'(x)\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[g(x)-h(x)]=\frac{d}{dx}g(x)-\frac{d}{dx}h(x)\)


Constant Multiplier Rule
\((c\cdot g(x))'=c\,g'(x)\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[c\,g(x)]=c\,\frac{d}{dx}g(x)\)




And two special derivatives: \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^x) = e^x\) and \(\frac{d}{dx}ln(x)=\frac{1}{x}\).

There’s more differentiation rules (product, quotient, chain rule).
They’re fun, but we won’t be reviewing them.

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Higher order derivatives


We can continue to take derivatives of derivatives.
The second derivative becomes the rate of change of the rate of change.
If we interpret the first derivative as velocity, then the second derivative is acceleration.



Notation:

Function: \(f(x) = y\)
1st derivative: \(f'(x)\) or \(\frac{dy}{dx}\)
2nd derivative: \(f''(x)\) or \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\)
nth derivative: \(f^{(n)}(x)\) or \(\frac{d^ny}{dx^n}\)

1) Researchers plotted dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration against water depth in a lake, and found the relationship was linear over the depth range sampled.










Write the equation for dissolved oxygen, \(DO\), as a function of depth.
Interpret the slope in a full sentence, including units.







NoteSolution

\(y\)-intercept: \(9\)
slope: \(\frac{3-9}{10-0} = \frac{-6}{10} = -0.6\)

\(DO(depth) = -0.6 \cdot depth + 9\)
b)
“For every additional meter of depth, dissolved oxygen concentration decreases by an average of 0.6 mg/L, starting from a surface concentration of about 9 mg/L.”



2) The growth of sharks can be modeled using von Bertalanffy curves. Scalloped hammerhead sharks in the Atlantic were found to have growth curves that follow the graph below.










What is the average slope from ages 0 to 8? From 20 to 30?
What are the units of the average slopes and why would they change for a shark as they get older?
How would you find the instantaneous slope for a shark at age 12? What is the closest approximation you can make with this data and graph?







NoteSolution





a)
The average slope from ages 0 to 8 can be calcualted by: \[ slope = \frac{155-40}{8-0} = 14.375\]
The average slope from ages 0 to 8 can be calcualted by: \[ slope = \frac{210-200}{30-20} =1 \]
This tells us that the average rate of change for sharks between the ages of 0 to 8 was 14.375. For the ages, 20 to 30 the average change was 1.

\]

8) Since 2010, a mountain glacier has been losing volume at an accelerating pace as regional temperatures rise. Researchers model the cumulative ice volume lost, \(V(t)\) (in km³), since monitoring began, as:
\[
V(t) = 0.5t^2 + 2t
\]
where \(t\) is years since 2010.

Use differentiation rules to find \(V'(t)\).
Evaluate \(V'(5)\). What does this value mean in the context of the glacier? State it as a full sentence, with units.
Now calculate the average rate of ice loss between \(t=4\) and \(t=8\).
Are the values from (b) and (c) the same? In your own words, explain conceptually why an “average” rate of change over an interval doesn’t have to match the “instantaneous” rate of change at a single point within it.







NoteSolution





(a) Using the power rule and sum rule: \[
V'(t) = t + 2
\]
(b) \[
V'(5) = 5 + 2 = 7 \ \frac{\text{km}^3}{\text{year}}
\]

“In 2015 (five years after monitoring began), the glacier was losing ice at an instantaneous rate of about 7 km³ per year.”

(c) \[
V(4) = 0.5(4)^2+2(4) = 16, \qquad V(8) = 0.5(8)^2+2(8) = 48
\] \[
\text{average rate of change} = \frac{V(8)-V(4)}{8-4} = \frac{48-16}{4} = 8 \ \frac{\text{km}^3}{\text{year}}
\]
(d) The two values are close, but not the same (7 vs. 8 km³/year). The average rate of change smooths the ice loss out over the entire 4-year window from \(t=4\) to \(t=8\), while the instantaneous rate captures the exact pace of loss at the single moment \(t=5\).

Derivative Rules

Explain how to find the derivative of the following functions. Be sure to explicitly denote which derivative rules (constant, multiple, sum, product, chain, etc.) you would use. For extra practice, have a try at solving them!


\(\large f(x)=\sqrt{(x+3)}\)

 We can use chain rule to compute this one, with the outer function being \(\sqrt(u)\) and ithe inner function being \(x+3\). We can compute each of these derivatives using the power rule. We obtain that<>
 \[
f'(x)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{(x+3)}}
\] 

\(h(a)=\frac{\exp^{-a}}{a^2-5}\)

 First we would use the quotient rule then to solve for the individual derivatives. The individual derivatives will require us to use the chain rule (for the numerator) and the power rule (for the denominator). We obtain that 
 \[
h'(a)=\frac{-(a^2-5)e^{-a}-(2a)e^{-a}}{(a^2-5)^2}
\] 

\(g(t)=\left(\frac{5t^3+2}{2(t^2-2)}\right)^6\)

 First chain rule. In the \(u\)-substitution we have to use the quotient and power rules. 
 \[\begin{align}
g(t)&=\left(\frac{5t^3+2}{2(t^2-2)}\right)^6 \\
g(t)&=u(t)^6  &u=\frac{5t^3+2}{2(t^2-2)}\\
g'(t)&=6(u(t))^5\times u'(t)  &\frac{du}{dt}=\frac{2(t^2-2)15t^2-4t(5t^3+2)}{(2(t^2-2))^2} \\
g'(t)&=6(u(t))^5* \frac{2(t^2-2)15t^2-4t(5t^3+2)}{(2(t^2-2))^2} \\
g'(t)&=6\left(\frac{5t^3+2}{2(t^2-2)}\right)^5\frac{2(t^2-2)15t^2-4t(5t^3+2)}{(2(t^2-2))^2}
\end{align}\]

The function \(f(x)\) has a positive derivative whenever it is increasing, this happens over the interval (-2,0). This is indicated as the blue interval on the graph below.

Find the critical points of the following function and determine whether they are maxima or minima:

\[
f(x) = 2x^3-5x^2+3x-12.
\]
 To do this we neeed to first find the critical points by solving \(f'(x)=0\) and then use the second derivative test on the critical points we find to determine if they are a maxima or a minima. Computing the first derivative using the power rule we have that 
 \[
f'(x)=6x^2-10x+3=0
\] 
 Then, using the quadratic formula to solve this equation we get that the critical points of \(f(x)\) are \(x\approx 1.27\) and \(x\approx 0.39\). 
 Next, the second derivative is \(f''(x)=12x-10\), and evaluating this at the critical points we get that \[f''(1.27)>0 \ \text{ and } \ f''(0.39)<0\] 
 Therefore, based on the first and second order conditions, there are two optimas for this function at \(x\approx 1.27\) and \(x\approx 0.39\). Plugging these values into the second order derivative we can see that \(x\approx 0.39\) is a maximum and \(x\approx 1.27\) is a minimum. 



Let’s solve the canonical Gordon-Schaefer fisheries production model. This model formed the basis of fisheries management for half a century and is still a widely used model. It starts by defining the change in the abundance or biomass of fish by the logistic growth equation:
\[\begin{equation}
\frac{dB}{dt}=rB(t)(1-\frac{B(t)}{K})
\end{equation}\]
where \(B\) is biomass, \(t\) is time, \(r\) is the intrinsic growth rate, and \(K\) is the carrying capacity.
Next, fishers catch fish based on their effort \(E\) (constant), technological ability \(q\) (constant as well and also called the catchability coefficient), and the amount of fish \(B\). For simplicity, we use an easy multiplicative form:
\[
Y(t)=qEB(t)
\]
This catch rate takes away from the growth of the fish stock, thus we can subtract it from the logistic growth equation 1.
\[\begin{equation}
\frac{dB}{dt}=rB(t)(1-\frac{B(t)}{K})-Y(t)
\end{equation}\]
a) Fishery managers are interested in finding the equilibrium level of biomass and harvest. We can set \(\frac{dB}{dt}=0\). Solve for the equilibrium biomass in terms of K,q,r,E.
 Substituting \(Y(t)\) in \(\frac{dB}{dt}\) and solving for B we obtain: \[
\begin{align}
0&=rB(1-\frac{B}{K})-qEB \\
qEB&=rB(1-\frac{B}{K})\\
qE&=r(1-\frac{B}{K})\\
\frac{rB}{K}&=r-qE \\
B&=K(1-\frac{qE}{r}).
\end{align}
\] 
b) Substitute the equilibrium biomass you found in (a) into the catch equation.
 Making this substitution we obtain \[
\begin{align}
Y&=qEB \\
&=qEK(1-\frac{qE}{r})\\
&=qEK-\frac{q^2E^2K}{r}.
\end{align}
\] 
c) What effort leads to a maximum sustainable yield? Maximize the equation from b) with respect to effort \(E\).
 Let’s take the derivative of the previous equation with respet to \(E\): \[
\begin{align}
\frac{dY}{dE}&= \frac{d}{dE} qEK-\frac{q^2E^2K}{r}\\
   &= qK-\frac{2q^2EK}{r}.
\end{align}
\] 
 To find the effort \(E\) that leads to the maximum yield we find the critical points: \[
\begin{align}
qK-\frac{2q^2EK}{r} = 0 &\Rightarrow qK =\frac{2q^2EK}{r} \\
                        &\Rightarrow  E^* = \frac{r}{2q}.
\end{align}
\] 
d) Interpret what you found in c). What are the two variables that drive fisher harvest levels?
 The amount of effort that leads to the most amount of catch is driven entirely by the rate of growth of fish stocks and the ability of fishers to catch them. If \(q\) catchability goes up, fishers become more efficient and need less effort to reach max harvest. Faster growing species allow for more growth and thus more effort to catch them. 
e) Calculate what is the maximum sustainable yield by substituting the optimal harvest level into the harvest equation.
 Doing this substitution we obtain that the maximum sustainable yield is \[\begin{align}
Y_{\text{max}}=\frac{qrK}{2q}-\frac{q^2(\frac{r}{2q})^2K}{r}\\
Y_{\text{max}}=\frac{rK}{2}-\frac{rK}{4}\\
Y_{\text{max}}=\frac{Kr}{4}.
\end{align}\]

Rules for differentiation (4)

Product Rule
Let \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) be differentiable functions. Then
\[
\large
\frac{d}{dx}[f(x)*g(x)]=f(x)g'(x)+g(x)f'(x)
\]
What this is saying:

Breakdown multiplication into two separate functions
Then take the first function times the derivative of the second, and add the second function times the derivative of the first.

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Product rule example

✏️ Find the derivative of \(y=2x(x^2+3x)\).
We have that:
\[
\begin{align}
y&=2x(x^2+3x) \\[3px]
y&=\overbrace{2x}^{f(x)}\overbrace{(x^2+3x)}^{g(x)} &\text{Break into two functions}\\[3px]
\frac{dy}{dx}&=\overbrace{2x}^{f(x)}\overbrace{(2x+3)}^{g'(x)}+\overbrace{2}^{f'(x)}\overbrace{(x^2+3x)}^{g(x)} &\text{Apply Power Rule}\\[3px]
\frac{dy}{dx}&=6x^2+12x  &\text{Algebra clean up}
\end{align}
\]
What is another way we could have computed this derivative?

\]

Composition of functions

If we have two functions \(f\) and \(g\), the composition of \(f\) and \(g\) is
\[f\circ g (x) = f(g(x)).\]
This means that the output of \(g(x)\) is now the input of \(f(x)\). In other words, composition of functions means applying one function to the result of another.


Examples
✏️ Let \(f(x) = x^2\) and \(g(x) = 2x+3\). What is \(f\circ g (x)\)?
 
✏️ Let \(h(x) = \sqrt{ 3x^2 + 10}\). How can we write \(h\) as a composition of functions?

Composition of functions

If we have two functions \(f\) and \(g\), the composition of \(f\) and \(g\) is
\[f\circ g (x) = f(g(x)).\]
This means that the output of \(g(x)\) is now the input of \(f(x)\). In other words, composition of functions means applying one function to the result of another.

Examples
✏️ Let \(f(x) = x^2\) and \(g(x) = 2x+3\). What is \(f\circ g (x)\)?
We have that \(f\circ g (x)  = (2x+3)^2\).
✏️ Let \(h(x) = \sqrt{ 3x^2 + 10}\). How can we write \(h\) as a composition of functions?
If we make \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\) and \(g(x) = 3x^2 +10\) then we have that \(f\circ g (x) = \sqrt{ 3x^2 + 10}.\)

Chain rule example

✏️ What is the derivative of \(y = (x^3 -2)^2\)? Let’s use a trick called \(u\)-substitution.

Identify the inner function and label it as \(u\). Rewrite \(y\) in terms of \(u\):

\[
\begin{align}
y &= (x^3-2)^2 \\
u &= x^3-2 \\
y &= u^2
\end{align}
\]

Take the derivative of \(y\) with respect to \(u\) and substitute \(u\):

\[\frac{dy}{du} = 2u = 2(x^3-2).\]

And the derivative of \(u\) with respect to \(x\):

\[\frac{du}{dx} = 3x^2.\]

Put everything back into the chain rule and simplify:

\[
\begin{align}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= \frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx} \\
              &= 2(x^3-2)(3x^2)
              = 6x^5 -12x^2.
\end{align}
\]

The number \(e\)

The number \(e\) is a constant in mathematics, it is approximately \(e\approx 2.72\), but really its decimals continue infinitely without any pattern.

It’s exact value can be described as \[
e = \lim_{n\to \infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^n.

Like any other number, \(e\) follows normal power properties
\[
\begin{align}
e^{x+y}&=&e^x\cdot e^y \\

e^{x-y}&=&\frac{e^x}{e^y}\\
e^{rx}&=&(e^x)^r

\]

How quickly is the human population rising right now?

Von Foersters et al. (1960) used the following function to describe the increase in human population over time:
\[
x(t)=\frac{1}{c-\beta t}
\]
Where \(c=9.833*10^{-3}\), \(\beta=4.849*10^{-6}\), and \(x\) is the total human population in millions at year \(t\).

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Use derivatives to find the answers!

- How quickly was the human population increasing in 1450?

“How quickly” are code words for “take the first derivative” of \(x(t)=\frac{1}{c-\beta t}\). Let’s do that:
\[
\begin{align}
x(t)&=\frac{1}{c-\beta t} \\
x(t)&=(c-\beta t)^{-1} &\text{Rearrange} \\
\frac{dx}{dt}&=\beta(c-\beta t)^{-2} &\text{Chain and Power Rule}\\
\end{align}
\]


Since the question is asking for how quickly was the population increasing in 1450 we need to evaluate the derivative at \(t=1450\). This is \[x'(1450)=.61\]
So, human population in 1450 was increasing at a rate of .61 million per year.

\[x'(2024) = \beta(c-\beta 2024)^{-2} = 13,980.\]
So, human population in 2024 will be increasing at a rate of 13,980 million per year according to this model.


After some investigation, human population is estimated to be growing at about 0.85% per year, which is around 70 million more people every year.

Local maxima and minima of funcitons

A funciton \(f(x)\) has…

a local maximum at \(p\) if \(f(p)\) is greater than or equal to the values of \(f\) for points near \(p\).



a local minimum at \(p\) if \(f(p)\) is less than or equal to the values of \(f\) for points near \(p\).




a critical point \(p\) if \(f'(p)=0\). The value \(f(p)\) at a critital point \(p\) is called a critical value.



Finding critical points helps us solve optimization problems: every maximum and miniumum occurs at a critical point.

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Finding maxima/minima

1) Find critical points with the 1st derivative:

If \(f(x)\) has a local maximum or minimum at \(p\) then \(f'(p)\) =0.
This means that we need to look for local max/min among critical points (the values for \(x\) for which \(f'(x)=0\)).



2) Apply the 2nd derivative test to critical points:

Whether a critical point is a maximum or minimum requires us to test if the function is concave up or concave down around that point.
If \(f'(p)=0\) and \(f''(p)<0\) then \(f(x)\) has a local maximum at \(p\).
If \(f'(x)=0\) and \(f''(x)>0\), then \(f(x)\) has a local minimum at \(p\).

Example

Find critical points with 1st derivative:

\[
\begin{align}
f(x)&=x^3-12x+2 \\
f'(x)&=3x^2-12 \\
x^*&=-2  & x^*=2
\end{align}
\]



Apply 2nd derivative test to critical points:

\[
\begin{align}
f''(x)&=6x \\
f''(-2)&<0  &f''(2)>0
\end{align}
\]



By the first order conditions we know that \(x=2\) and \(x=-2\) are the critical points of the function.
The second order conditions inform us that \(f(x)\) has a local maximum at \(x=-2\) and a local minimum at \(x=2\).

Policy A provides \(\sqrt{10x+4}\) benefits where \(x\) is the dollar spent on interventions. Policy B provides \(\sqrt{20x+4}\) benefits for every dollar spent. However, each policy has a cost associated with each. Policy A has a constant linear cost at \(2x\) and Policy B has a constant linear cost at \(3x\).

a) Which policy is cheaper?

b) Find the optimal amount of interventions dollars to spend for each policy. Consider both costs and benefits. [Hint: Remember \(\sqrt{}\) is just \(x^{\frac{1}{2}}\). You can use exponent rules to help solve]

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Solution to exercise 3

a. Which policy is cheaper?
Policy A is cheaper: it costs \(2x\) vs. \(3x\) for Policy B.
b. Optimal spending = maximizing net benefits
For this, we need to create a function representing the net benefits for each policy:
\[
\begin{align}
B_A (x) &= \sqrt{10x+4} - 2x & \text{net benefits for policy A,}\\
B_A (x) &= \sqrt{20x+4} - 3x & \text{net benefits for policy B}.
\end{align}
\] Solving for critical points and applying the second derivative test we get that \(B_A\) benefits are maximized when \(x_A=\frac{9}{40}=0.225\) dollars are spent and \(B_B\) benefits are maximized when \(x_B=\frac{16}{45}\approx0.356\) dollars are spent.
b. Which policy provides the most benefits?
If we compare the maximum net benefits offered by each policy we get \[
B_A (0.225) = 2.05\  \text{ and }
B_B (\frac{16}{45})\  \approx 2.27.
\]
So policy B provides the maximum net benefits.
d. Which policy should the city pursue?
Because Policy B yields the larger maximal net benefit (≈2.27), the City of Santa Barbara should probably pursue Policy B, assuming there are no restrictions in how much money they can invest in the policy.

Functions are like baking recipes

What is a function?

For each combination of independent variables, there is exactly one (and only one) value of the dependent variable.
Vertical line test
If you run a vertical line perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis and see where it intersects the graph of a function, then it should only intersect it once at every value of \(x\).

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Continuity

Intuitively, a function is continuous if there are no ‘breaks’ in the graph of the function. This means you are able to draw the whole graph without lifting your pencil.
To define it formally we need to understand limits.

A function is discontinuous if it’s not continuous! So there are ‘breaks’ or ‘gaps’ in its graph.




Continuous

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Limits

Definition
We say a number \(L\) is the limit of a function \(f(x)\) as its variable \(x\) approaches a number \(c\), if the function’s output values \(f(x)\) approach \(L\) when \(x\) get closer to \(c\).

We write this symbolically as:
\[
\large
\lim_{x\to c} f(x)=L
\]

We read this as: “The limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches \(c\) is \(L\).”

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Example: numerical

What is the limit of \(f(x)=2x^2-4\) as \(x\) approaches 2?
We need to examine the values of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) gets closer to 2 from both sides.










From both directions it looks like \(f(x)\) converges to 4.
So, we say that “The limit of \(2x^2-4\) as \(x\) approaches 2 is 4” and we can write it like this:
\[
\lim_{x\to 2}(2x^2-4)=4
\]

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Example: graph

What is the limit of \(f(x)=2x^2-4\) as \(x\) approaches 2?

From both directions it looks like \(f(x)\) converges to 4.
So, \(\lim_{x\to 2}(2x^2-4)=4\).

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Continuity revisited



A function \(f(x)\) is continuous at \(x=c\) if
\[
\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c).
\]
So, if a function is continuous, we just need to evaluate the function to obtain the limit.
Example
\(f(x) = 2x^2-4\) is a continuous function. So we can obtain the limit as \(x\to 2\) by evaluating the function
\[\lim_{x\to 2}(2x^2-4)= f(2) = 4.\]

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Limit at a discontinuity


Discontinuous functions can still have limits at a discontinuity.

Example
Let \[
f(x) = x+1 , \text{ if x $\neq$ 2}
\]
✏️ Draw a graph of \(f(x)\). Then try calculating \(\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)\).









The value \(f(2)\) may not exist, but we can still find a limit because \(f(x)\) consistently approaches 3 from both directions as \(x\to 2\).

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
No limit at a discontinuity


But other times discontinuous functions don’t have a limit at a discontinuity.

Example
The function \(|x|\) is the absolute value function. It is such that
\[
|x| =
\begin{cases}
x, & \text{ if } x\geq 0 \\
-x, & \text{ if } x <0
\end{cases}
.
\]


✏️ Is the function \(f(x) = \frac{|x-2|}{x-2}\) continuous at \(x=2\)?
✏️ Try calculating: \[
\lim_{x\to 2}\frac{|x-2|}{x-2}.
\]

Hint: Try to do numerical approximations or draw the graph of this function.

Is the function \(f(x) = \frac{|x-2|}{x-2}\) continuous at \(x=2\)?
This function is not even defined at \(x=2\) since it would require us to divide by zero, which is undefined.


Try calculating \(\lim_{x\to 2}\frac{|x-2|}{x-2}\).
Let’s investigate:

title: Bren Math Workshop

No limit at a discontinuity

The function \(\frac{|x-2|}{x-2}\) approaches different values from either side at \(x=2\).



Therefore… the limit does not exist!

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Side limits

Though the function \(f(x) = \frac{|x-2|}{x-2}\) had no limit at \(x=2\), it clearly was approaching certain values when we considered only values of \(x\) from one side or the other:











In this case we say that


\[
\lim_{x\to 2^-} f(x) = -1
\]
The limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches 2 from the left is -1.

Notice the small - subscript on the 2.

\[
\lim_{x\to 2^+} f(x) = 1
\]
The limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches 2 from the right is 1.

Notice the small + subscript on the 2.

Start with a point \((x,f(x))\) on the graph.
A nearby point can be \((x+\Delta x, f(x+\Delta x))\), where \(\Delta x\) is a short distance from \(x\).

The average slope between \((x,f(x))\) and \((x+\Delta x, f(x+\Delta x))\) is given by
 \[\text{average slope} = \frac{f(x+\Delta x) - f(x)}{(x+\Delta x)-x} = \frac{f(x+\Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x}.\]

Tangent lines

What if we let \(\Delta x=0\)?
Then we would have a slope line that only touches the graph at exactly \(x\). 


These very special types of lines are called tangent lines.

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Derivative definition

Remember the slope of the line that passes between two points \((x_1, y_1)\) and \((x_2, y_2)\) is:
\[\text{slope}=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}.\]

If we have a function \(f(x)\), then \((x,f(x))\) represents a point on its graph.


Choose a different point on the graph that is \(\Delta x\) away: \((x+\Delta x,f(x+\Delta x))\).


Plug these pointson the graph of \(f(x)\) into the slope equation:
\[
\text{slope}=\frac{f(x+\Delta x)-f(x)}{\Delta x}.
\]


When we let \(\Delta x \to 0\) we get the slope of the tangent line at \(x\)
 \[
\large
f'(x)=\lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \frac{f(x+\Delta x)-f(x)}{\Delta x}
\] 
This is the derivative of \(f\) at \(x\). Also denoted \(\frac{df}{dx}\).

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Rules for differentiation (1)

Constant Rule
Let \(c\) be a constant (so, a number). If \(f(x) = c\), then \(f'(x)=0\). Equivalently
\[\frac{d}{dx}c = 0\]
Power Rule
Let \(n\) be a (real) number, if \(f(x)= x^n\), then \(f'(x) = nx^{n-1}\). Equivalently \[
\frac{d}{dx}[x^n]
=nx^{n-1}.
\]

Examples
\[
\begin{align}
&y=100 & &f(x)=x^5 & &f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2}
\end{align}
\]

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Rules for differentiation (2)

Sum and Difference Rules

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Rules for differentiation (2)

Sum and Difference Rules
Let \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) be differentiable functions. Then \[
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dx}[f(x)+g(x)]=\frac{d}{dx}f(x)+\frac{d}{dx}g(x) \\
\frac{d}{dx}[f(x)-g(x)]=\frac{d}{dx}f(x)-\frac{d}{dx}g(x)
\end{align}
\]
😵All this says is: if the function has pieces that are added or subtracted you can take the derivative of each individual piece and add those derivatives.

Example
\[
f(x)=x^3-x^2-15
\]

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Rules for differentiation (3)

Constant Multiplier Rule

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Rules for differentiation (3)

Constant Multiplier Rule
The derivative of a constant \(c\) multiplied by a function \(f(x)\) is the same as the constant multiplied by the derivative:
\[\frac{d}{dx}[kf(x)] = k\frac{d}{dx}f(x)\]

Example
\[
y=x^2+\sqrt{2}x-\frac{8}{x}+4
\]

Differentiation Rule
\(f'(x)\) notation

Constant Rule
\(f(x)=c \Rightarrow f'(x)=0\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[c]=0\)


Power Rule
\(f(x)=x^n \Rightarrow f'(x)=n x^{n-1}\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[x^n]=n x^{n-1}\)


Sum Rule
\((g(x)+h(x))'=g'(x)+h'(x)\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[g(x)+h(x)]=\frac{d}{dx}g(x)+\frac{d}{dx}h(x)\)


Difference Rule
\((g(x)-h(x))' = g'(x)-h'(x)\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[g(x)-h(x)]=\frac{d}{dx}g(x)-\frac{d}{dx}h(x)\)


Constant Multiplier Rule
\((c\cdot g(x))'=c\,g'(x)\)
\(\frac{d}{dx}[c\,g(x)]=c\,\frac{d}{dx}g(x)\)

\[

\boxed{21{,}600{,}000\text{ m}^3}

\]
Step 2: Convert liters to milliliters

Step 3: Divide to get the new concentration

\boxed{6\text{ mg/mL}}

8) One microgram (μg) is equivalent to \(1/10^6\) grams and one meter cubed (m³) is equivalent to 1000 liters. A pollutant concentration is 12 μg/mL. Convert this to kg/m³.






NoteSolution





Given

Concentration = 12 μg/mL
\(1\ \mu\text{g} = 10^{-6}\text{ g}\) and \(1\text{ m}^3 = 1000\text{ L}\)

Step 1: Find a conversion factor from micrograms to kilograms
\[
1\ \mu\text{g} = 10^{-6}\text{ g} = 10^{-9}\text{ kg} \implies \frac{10^{-9}\text{ kg}}{1\ \mu\text{g}}
\]
Step 2: Find a conversion factor from m³ to mL
\[
1\text{ m}^3 = 1000\text{ L} = 10^{6}\text{ mL} \implies \frac{10^{6}\text{ mL}}{1\text{ m}^3}
\]
Step 3: Multiply by the conversion factors, group numbers and units, and simplify
\[\begin{align*}
12\ \frac{\mu\text{g}}{\text{mL}} &= 12\ \frac{\mu\text{g}}{\text{mL}} \cdot \frac{10^{-9}\text{ kg}}{1\ \mu\text{g}} \cdot \frac{10^{6}\text{ mL}}{1\text{ m}^3}\\
&= \left(12 \times 10^{-9} \times 10^{6}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{\mu\text{g}}{\text{mL}}\cdot\frac{\text{kg}}{\mu\text{g}}\cdot\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{m}^3}\right)\\
&= 0.012\ \frac{\text{kg}}{\text{m}^3}
\end{align*}\]
Answer
\[
\boxed{0.012\text{ kg/m}^3}
\]



9) A watershed receives 45 mm/year of precipitation over an area of 1,800 km². Find the total annual volume of precipitation in m³/year.






NoteSolution





Given

Precipitation = 45 mm/year
Watershed area = 1,800 km²

Step 1: Convert precipitation to meters
\[
45\text{ mm} = \frac{45}{1000} = 0.045\text{ m}
\]
Step 2: Convert area to square meters
\[
1,800\text{ km}^2 = 1,800(1,000)^2
\]
\[
= 1.8 \times 10^9\text{ m}^2
\]
Step 3: Calculate the annual precipitation volume
Volume is calculated as:
\[
V = P \times A
\]
Substitute the values:
\[
V = (0.045)(1.8 \times 10^9)
\]
\[
V = 8.1 \times 10^7\text{ m}^3/\text{year}
\]
Answer
\[
\boxed{81,000,000\text{ m}^3/\text{year}}
\]

Company A: 14.6 barrels spilled (with 9.3 barrels recovered)
Company B: 692 liters spilled (94% recovered)
Company C: 18.1 gallons spilled (0% recovered)

What is the total unrecovered amount of oil spilled into the watershed that year, in barrels. Use the conversion 1 barrel = 42 gallons = 159 liters and a calculator when needed.






NoteSolution





Given

Company A: 14.6 barrels spilled, 9.3 barrels recovered
Company B: 692 L spilled, 94% recovered
Company C: 18.1 gallons spilled, 0% recovered
Conversions: 1 barrel = 42 gallons = 159 liters

Step 1: Company A’s unrecovered oil (already in barrels)
\[

\[
692 \times (1 - 0.94) = 41.52\text{ L unrecovered}

\[
41.52\text{ L} \times \frac{1\text{ barrel}}{159\text{ L}} = 0.26\text{ barrels}
\]
Step 3: Company C’s unrecovered oil, converted to barrels
\[
18.1\text{ gal} \times \frac{1\text{ barrel}}{42\text{ gal}} = 0.43\text{ barrels}
\]
Step 4: Add up all three companies’ unrecovered oil
\[
5.3 + 0.26 + 0.43 = 5.99\text{ barrels}
\]
Answer
\[
\boxed{5.99\text{ barrels unrecovered}}
\]






11) A city is considering a curbside compost pickup program. A survey of households estimates the monthly demand for the service as \[
P = 25 - 0.05Q
\] where \(Q\) = number of households subscribed in hundreds and \(P\) = the monthly fee ($) a household is willing to pay.










In one sentence, describe what the graph shows.
Interpret what the \(y\)-intercept means in this context.
Interpret what the \(x\)-intercept means in this context.







NoteSolution





a) On the \(x\) axis we have hunderds of households subscribed and on the \(y\) axis we have monthly fee in dollars. The plot shows a linear demand curve. We can see that as the monthly fee drops, more households are willing to subscribe to the compost program.
b)
The \(y\)-intercept is $25/month, this is the highest fee at which any household is still willing to subscribe. Above $25, quantity demanded drops to zero.
c)
The \(x\)-intercept is \(Q=500\) (i.e., 500 hundred = 50,000 households). This is the number of households that would subscribe if the service were free. This is the maximum possible demand for the program.

12\ \frac{\mu\text{g}}{\text{mL}} &= 12\ \frac{\mu\text{g}}{\text{mL}} \cdot \frac{10^{-9}\text{ kg}}{1\ \mu\text{g}} \cdot \frac{10^{6}\text{ mL}}{1\text{ m}^3}\\
&= \left(12 \times 10^{-9} \times 10^{6}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{\mu\text{g}}{\text{mL}}\cdot\frac{\text{kg}}{\mu\text{g}}\cdot\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{m}^3}\right)\\
&= 0.012\ \frac{\text{kg}}{\text{m}^3}
\end{align*}\]
Answer
\[
\boxed{0.012\text{ kg/m}^3}
\]



9) A watershed receives 45 mm/year of precipitation over an area of 1,800 km². Find the total annual volume of precipitation in m³/year.






NoteSolution





Given

Precipitation = 45 mm/year
Watershed area = 1,800 km²

Step 1: Convert precipitation to meters
\[
45\text{ mm} = \frac{45}{1000} = 0.045\text{ m}
\]
Step 2: Convert area to square meters
\[
1,800\text{ km}^2 = 1,800(1,000)^2
\]
\[
= 1.8 \times 10^9\text{ m}^2
\]
Step 3: Calculate the annual precipitation volume
Volume is calculated as:
\[
V = P \times A
\]
Substitute the values:
\[
V = (0.045)(1.8 \times 10^9)
\]
\[
V = 8.1 \times 10^7\text{ m}^3/\text{year}
\]
Answer
\[
\boxed{81,000,000\text{ m}^3/\text{year}}
\]



10) You are combining information from multiple sources to estimate the total annual oil spilled in a watershed, reported by different companies. The following are reported for the year:

Company A: 14.6 barrels spilled (with 9.3 barrels recovered)
Company B: 692 liters spilled (94% recovered)
Company C: 18.1 gallons spilled (0% recovered)

What is the total unrecovered amount of oil spilled into the watershed that year, in barrels. Use the conversion 1 barrel = 42 gallons = 159 liters and a calculator when needed.






NoteSolution





Given

Company A: 14.6 barrels spilled, 9.3 barrels recovered
Company B: 692 L spilled, 94% recovered
Company C: 18.1 gallons spilled, 0% recovered
Conversions: 1 barrel = 42 gallons = 159 liters

Step 1: Company A’s unrecovered oil (already in barrels)
\[
14.6 - 9.3 = 5.3\text{ barrels}
\]
Step 2: Company B’s unrecovered oil, converted to barrels
\[
692 \times (1 - 0.94) = 41.52\text{ L unrecovered}
\]
\[
41.52\text{ L} \times \frac{1\text{ barrel}}{159\text{ L}} = 0.26\text{ barrels}
\]
Step 3: Company C’s unrecovered oil, converted to barrels
\[
18.1\text{ gal} \times \frac{1\text{ barrel}}{42\text{ gal}} = 0.43\text{ barrels}
\]
Step 4: Add up all three companies’ unrecovered oil
\[
5.3 + 0.26 + 0.43 = 5.99\text{ barrels}
\]
Answer
\[
\boxed{5.99\text{ barrels unrecovered}}
\]

Metric units are built from a base unit (like meters, grams, or liters) plus a prefix that scales it by a power of 10.



The factor indicates how many times to multiply the base unit by 10.
Example: 1 km = \(10^3\) m = 1000 m, and 1 cm = \(10^{-2}\) m = 0.01 m.

The factor indicates how many times to multiply the base unit by 10.

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Metric prefixes

Example. Convert 750 mL into L.


Starting at milli and ending at base, we move 3 rows up the table:
milli → centi → deci → base
So we divide by \(10^3\):
\[\begin{align*}
750 \text{ mL} &= \frac{750}{10^3} \text{ L} \\
&= 0.75 \text{ L}
\end{align*}\]

Exercise. Convert 4.7 km into cm.


Starting at kilo and ending at centi, we move 5 rows down the table:
kilo → hecto → deka → base → deci → centi
So we multiply by \(10^5\):
\[\begin{align*}
4.7 \text{ km} &= 4.7 \times 10^5 \text{ cm} \\
&= 470{,}000 \text{ cm}
\end{align*}\]

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Converting areas and volumes

So far we’ve converted linear units (length). What about area (squared units) and volume (cubed units)?


To convert area units, square the linear conversion factor.
To convert volume units, cube the linear conversion factor.

Since \(1 \text{ m} = 100 \text{ cm}\):
\[\begin{align*}
1 \text{ m}^2 &= (100 \text{ cm})^2 = 100^2 \text{ cm}^2 = 10{,}000 \text{ cm}^2 \\
1 \text{ m}^3 &= (100 \text{ cm})^3 = 100^3 \text{ cm}^3 = 1{,}000{,}000 \text{ cm}^3
\end{align*}\]

Example. Convert \(3.5 \text{ m}^2\) into \(\text{cm}^2\).

The linear factor from meters to centimeters is \(10^2\) (2 rows down the metric prefix table). For area, we square this factor:

\[\begin{align*}
3.5 \text{ m}^2 &= 3.5 \times (10^2)^2 \text{ cm}^2 \\
&= 3.5 \times 10^4 \text{ cm}^2 \\
&= 35{,}000 \text{ cm}^2.
\end{align*}\]

The linear factor from meters to centimeters is \(10^2\) (2 rows down the metric prefix table). For volume, we cube this factor:

\[\begin{align*}
2 \text{ m}^3 &= 2 \times (10^2)^3 \text{ cm}^3 \\
&= 2 \times 10^6 \text{ cm}^3 \\
&= 2{,}000{,}000 \text{ cm}^3.

Dimensional analysis (unit conversions)

In dimensional analysis, we multiply initial units by a sequence of unit conversion factors to arrive at the final desired units.
Example: How many centimiters are there in 6 inches?
✏️ Let’s solve this together.

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Dimensional analysis (unit conversions)

In dimensional analysis, we multiply initial units by a sequence of unit conversion factors to arrive at the final desired units.
Example: How many centimiters are there in 6 inches?
We know: 1 inch = 2.54 cm. This gives us two unit conversion factors:
\[ \frac{2.54 \text{ cm}}{1 \text{ in}} \text{ and } \frac{1 \text{ in}}{2.54 \text{ cm}}.\] Important: the fraction the numerator and denominator represent the same quantity.
Then we multiply by the appropriate conversion factor and simplify:
\[\begin{align*}

6 \text{ in} &= 6 \text{ in} \cdot  \frac{2.54 \text{ cm}}{1 \text{ in}}\\
&= 6  \frac{2.54}{1} \cdot  \text{ in}\frac{\text{ cm}}{\text{ in}} \\
&= 15.24 \cancel{\text{ in}}\frac{\text{ cm}}{\cancel{\text{ in}}} \\
&= 15.24 \text{ cm}
\end{align*}\]

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Dimensional analysis (unit conversions)

Example. Convert \(100 \frac{g}{cm^3}\) into units of \(\frac{kg}{in^3}\), given that 1 cm3 = 0.061 in3.
✏️ Let’s solve this together.

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Dimensional analysis (unit conversions)

Example. Convert \(100 \frac{g}{cm^3}\) into units of \(\frac{kg}{in^3}\), given that 1 cm3 = 0.061 in3.
We need one unit conversion factor for \(g\): \(\frac{1 \text{ kg}}{1000 \text{ g}}\).
And another one for \(\text{cm}^3\): \(\frac{1 \text{ cm}^3}{0.061 \text{in}^3}\).
Then we multiply by the conversion factors and simplify
\[\begin{align*}

100 \frac{\text{ g}}{\text{cm}^3} &= 100 \frac{\text{ g}}{\text{cm}^3} \cdot \frac{1 \text{ cm}^3}{0.061 \text{ in}^3} \cdot \frac{1 \text{ kg}}{1000 \text{ g}}\\
&= 100 \frac{1}{0.061} \frac{1}{1000}\cdot \frac{\text{ g}}{\text{cm}^3} \frac{\text{ cm}^3}{ \text{ in}^3} \frac{ \text{ kg}}{\text{ g}}\\
&= \frac{1}{0.61} \cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{ g}}}{\cancel{\text{cm}^3}} \frac{\cancel{\text{ cm}^3}}{ \text{ in}^3} \frac{ \text{ kg}}{\cancel{\text{ g}}}\\
&=1.639\frac{kg}{in^3}.
\end{align*}\]

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Parts per million (ppm)


Parts per million (ppm) is another way of writing a fraction (just like percentage) but suited to very small concentrations (e.g. a contaminant in water or soil).


We have that:
\[
1\% = \frac{1}{100} \qquad \qquad 1 \text{ ppm} = \frac{1}{1{,}000{,}000}
\]
From these fractions we see we need 10,000 ppm to get 1%, so 1% = 10,000 ppm.
To convert percent → ppm, multiply percentage by 10,000. 
To convert ppm → percent, divide ppm by 10,000.

Functions

Functions are mathematical expressions that tell us how input values are related to output values.

For example, \(y = 3x-5\) is a function that tells us the value of y at any value of x. In this scenario, we would probably say y is a function of x.
Could you also rewrite it and say x is a function of y?
Here, with no knowledge of what’s an input and what’s an output, sure - but usually in environmental science we specify the input variable(s), and the output variable(s) carefully.
What follows is the expression in the format of:

Also: output variable = dependent variable and input variable = independent variable.

title: Core Course Exercise Bank — Draft
text:
1. Solving simple equations

ESM 201
Source: instructor note — “basic algebra rather than actual calc” is the top concern for 201.
Exercise 1 (Intro). An organism’s daily energy budget splits intake between growth, metabolism, and reproduction: Intake = Growth + Metabolism + Reproduction. If daily intake is 120 kcal, metabolism is 50 kcal, and reproduction is 15 kcal, solve for Growth.






NoteSolution





\(120 = G + 50 + 15 \Rightarrow G = 120 - 65 = 55\) kcal/day.



Exercise 2 (Medium). The maximum sustainable yield of a harvested population is \(H = \dfrac{rK}{4}\). If the sustainable harvest is \(H = 80\) individuals/year and the carrying capacity is \(K = 800\), solve for the intrinsic growth rate \(r\).






NoteSolution





\(80 = \dfrac{r \cdot 800}{4} = 200r \Rightarrow r = 0.4\) per year.



Exercise 3 (Hard). The logistic per-capita growth rate is \(r\left(1 - \dfrac{N}{K}\right)\). If this rate equals \(0.02\) when \(N = 750\) and \(K = 1000\), solve for \(r\).






NoteSolution





\(1 - \dfrac{750}{1000} = 0.25\), so \(0.25r = 0.02 \Rightarrow r = 0.08\) per year.





ESM 202
Source: instructor note — unit conversions are the top priority, but basic algebra (e.g., mass-balance/dilution equations) is the step just before a conversion.
Exercise 4 (Intro). A tank’s mass balance is Mass in = Mass out + Mass accumulated. If 50 kg entered and 30 kg accumulated, solve for the mass that left.






NoteSolution





\(50 = \text{out} + 30 \Rightarrow \text{out} = 20\) kg.



Exercise 5 (Medium). To dilute a stock solution, \(C_1V_1 = C_2V_2\). How much of a 12% stock solution is needed to make 3 L of a 2% solution?






NoteSolution





\(12\% \cdot V_1 = 2\% \cdot 3\text{ L} \Rightarrow V_1 = \dfrac{2 \times 3}{12} = 0.5\) L.



Exercise 6 (Hard). A steady-state concentration balance is \(3(C - 5) + 2C = 40\) (mg/L). Solve for \(C\).






NoteSolution





\(3C - 15 + 2C = 40 \Rightarrow 5C = 55 \Rightarrow C = 11\) mg/L.





ESM 203
Source: real formula from the ESM 203 quiz sheet — “Change in storage per unit time = precipitation − actual ET − river outflows.”
Exercise 7 (Intro). At steady state, \(0 = P - AET - Q\). If \(P = 900\) mm/y and \(AET = 550\) mm/y, solve for streamflow \(Q\).






NoteSolution





\(Q = 900 - 550 = 350\) mm/y.



Exercise 8 (Medium). The aridity index is \(AI = P/PET\). If \(AI = 0.35\) and \(PET = 1400\) mm/y, solve for \(P\).






NoteSolution





\(P = 0.35 \times 1400 = 490\) mm/y.



Exercise 9 (Hard). In a watershed, actual evapotranspiration is 60% of precipitation: \(AET = 0.6P\). At steady state, \(0 = P - 0.6P - Q\), and \(Q = 320\) mm/y. Solve for \(P\).






NoteSolution





\(P - 0.6P = 0.4P = 320 \Rightarrow P = 800\) mm/y.





ESM 204
Source: single-formula algebra drawn from real 204 material — Anna Pede’s elasticity emphasis (HW1), the inverse-demand “isolate P” rearrangement that also appears in the Day 1 lecture, and a breakeven (quadratic-formula) framing of the profit function used in HW2’s marginal-cost material. Kept to one formula and one unknown, unlike the Demand = Supply system exercises below, which have been moved to Topic 4 (Equation of a line) since solving for an equilibrium is really finding where two lines intersect.
Exercise 10 (Intro). Price elasticity of demand is \(\varepsilon = \dfrac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta P}\). A policy raises price by 15%, and demand is unit elastic (\(\varepsilon = -1\)). Solve for the percent change in quantity, \(\%\Delta Q\).






NoteSolution





\(\%\Delta Q = \varepsilon \times \%\Delta P = -1 \times 15\% = -15\%\).



Exercise 11 (Medium). Inverse demand is often written \(Q = \dfrac{a - P}{b}\). Isolate \(P\) in terms of \(Q\), \(a\), and \(b\).






NoteSolution





\(bQ = a - P \Rightarrow P = a - bQ\).



Exercise 12 (Hard). A firm’s profit is \(\pi(Q) = 40Q - 0.5Q^2 - 200\) (in $100s). At what output level(s) \(Q\) does the firm break even (\(\pi = 0\))? Use the quadratic formula.






NoteSolution





Set \(-0.5Q^2+40Q-200=0\), or equivalently \(Q^2-80Q+400=0\). Quadratic formula: \(Q=\dfrac{80\pm\sqrt{80^2-4(400)}}{2}=\dfrac{80\pm\sqrt{4800}}{2}\approx\dfrac{80\pm69.3}{2}\). So \(Q\approx74.6\) or \(Q\approx5.4\) — the firm breaks even at these two output levels (and earns positive profit for \(Q\) between them).

title: Core Course Exercise Bank — Draft
text:
2. Percentages

ESM 202
Source: instructor note — “conversions between ppm and percent” called out as the single most important skill in 202.
Exercise 13 (Intro). Convert 250 ppm to a percentage.






NoteSolution





\(250 \text{ ppm} = \dfrac{250}{10{,}000}\% = 0.025\%\).



Exercise 14 (Medium). A water sample is 0.015% contaminant by mass. Express this in ppm.






NoteSolution





\(0.015\% \times 10{,}000 = 150\) ppm.



Exercise 15 (Hard). A 500 g soil sample is 2.4% organic matter by mass, and separately contains 380 ppm of a heavy metal. What is the ratio of organic matter mass to heavy metal mass in the sample?






NoteSolution





Organic matter: \(2.4\% \times 500\text{ g} = 12\) g. Heavy metal (ppm by mass = mg/kg): \(500\text{ g} = 0.5\text{ kg}\), so \(380 \text{ mg/kg} \times 0.5\text{ kg} = 190\text{ mg} = 0.19\) g. Ratio \(= 12 / 0.19 \approx 63.2\).





ESM 203
Source: real quiz-prep slide examples — relative humidity, aridity index, and runoff ratio (all percent-based quantities).
Exercise 16 (Intro). Saturation vapor pressure at 10°C is 1.23 kPa; actual vapor pressure is 0.37 kPa. Find the relative humidity.






NoteSolution





\(RH = 0.37/1.23 \approx 30.1\%\).



Exercise 17 (Medium). Annual precipitation is 620 mm/y and potential evapotranspiration is 1550 mm/y. Express the aridity index as a percent.






NoteSolution





\(AI = 620/1550 = 0.40 = 40\%\).



Exercise 18 (Hard). A watershed receives 950 mm/y of precipitation. Actual evapotranspiration is 65% of precipitation. What is the runoff ratio?






NoteSolution





\(AET = 0.65 \times 950 = 617.5\) mm/y. Runoff \(= 950 - 617.5 = 332.5\) mm/y. Runoff ratio \(= 332.5/950 = 35\%\).





ESM 204
Source: instructor emphasis on elasticity/percent-change reasoning (HW1’s elasticity question).
Exercise 19 (Intro). A policy raises the price of a good from $20 to $23. What is the percent change in price?






NoteSolution





\(\Delta P/P = 3/20 = 15\%\).



Exercise 20 (Medium). Quantity demanded falls from 500 to 425 units after the price increase above. What is the percent change in quantity?






NoteSolution





\(\Delta Q/Q = -75/500 = -15\%\).



Exercise 21 (Hard). Using the price change (+15%) and quantity change (−15%) above, compute the price elasticity of demand and state whether demand is elastic, unit elastic, or inelastic.






NoteSolution





\(\varepsilon = -15\%/15\% = -1\). \(|\varepsilon| = 1\), so demand is unit elastic.





ESM 201
Source: general population percent-change reasoning (supports the instructor’s “basic math” emphasis, applied to population counts).
Exercise 22 (Intro). A population of 240 individuals grows to 264 the next year. What is the percent increase?






NoteSolution





\(24/240 = 10\%\).



Exercise 23 (Medium). A population of 500 declines by 18%. What is the new population size?






NoteSolution





\(500 \times 0.82 = 410\).



Exercise 24 (Hard). A population grows 12% one year, then declines 12% the next. Starting from an index of 100, is the population back to its original size? Compute the net percent change.






NoteSolution





After +12%: \(112\). After −12%: \(112 \times 0.88 = 98.56\). Net change \(= -1.44\%\) — not back to the original size, because successive percent changes don’t cancel (the second change applies to a different base).

title: Core Course Exercise Bank — Draft
text:
3. Exponents

ESM 201
Source: instructor note — explicitly named exponent/fraction simplification (“\(2/k/2=\ldots\)”) as a top concern.
Exercise 25 (Intro). Simplify: \(k^5 / k^2\).






NoteSolution





\(k^5/k^2 = k^{5-2} = k^3\).



Exercise 26 (Medium). Simplify: \((k^3)^2 / k^4\).






NoteSolution





\((k^3)^2 = k^6\), so \(k^6/k^4 = k^2\).



Exercise 27 (Hard). A population’s growth factor per generation is \(\lambda = 1.2\). If \(N_0 = 50\) and after several generations \(N(t) = 50 \times (1.2)^2 \times (1.2)^3\), simplify the exponent expression and compute \(N(t)\).






NoteSolution





\((1.2)^2 \times (1.2)^3 = (1.2)^5 \approx 2.488\). \(N(t) = 50 \times 2.488 \approx 124.4\), i.e., about 124 individuals.





ESM 203
Source: the Teten formula from ESM 203 Assignment 2, which has the form \(e = 6.112\,e^{(\ldots)}\).
Exercise 28 (Intro). Simplify \(e^3 \times e^2\), and name the exponent rule used.






NoteSolution





\(e^3 \times e^2 = e^5\) (product of powers with the same base: add the exponents).



Exercise 29 (Medium). Given \(e^1 \approx 2.718\) and \(e^2 \approx 7.389\), find \(e^3\) using the product-of-powers rule (no calculator “\(e^x\)” button).






NoteSolution





\(e^3 = e^1 \times e^2 \approx 2.718 \times 7.389 \approx 20.09\).



Exercise 30 (Hard). Using the Tetens formula \(e_s = 6.112 \cdot e^{\left(\frac{17.67(T-273.15)}{T-29.65}\right)}\) (T in Kelvin), evaluate the saturation vapor pressure at \(T = 293.15\) K (20°C).






NoteSolution





Exponent: \(\dfrac{17.67 \times (293.15-273.15)}{293.15-29.65} = \dfrac{17.67 \times 20}{263.5} = \dfrac{353.4}{263.5} \approx 1.341\).
\(e^{1.341} \approx 3.823\). \(e_s = 6.112 \times 3.823 \approx 23.4\) hPa \(\approx 2.34\) kPa — matching the known real-world value for 20°C.





ESM 204
Source: HW4’s discount-rate sensitivity analysis, which is fundamentally repeated exponentiation of \((1+r)\).
Exercise 31 (Intro). Simplify \((1.05)^2 \times (1.05)^3\) as a single power of 1.05. If 1.05 is an annual growth factor, what does the result represent?






NoteSolution





\((1.05)^2 \times (1.05)^3 = (1.05)^5\) — growth compounded over 5 years.



Exercise 32 (Medium). A cost of $10,000 occurs in year 3. Using discount factor \(1/(1+r)^t\) with \(r = 0.06\), find its present value.






NoteSolution





\(1.06^3 \approx 1.191\). \(PV = 10{,}000/1.191 \approx \$8{,}397\).



Exercise 33 (Hard). Compare the present value of $5,000 received in year 10 under \(r=0.03\) vs. \(r=0.08\). By what percent does the higher discount rate reduce the present value?






NoteSolution





\(1.03^{10} \approx 1.344 \Rightarrow PV \approx 5000/1.344 \approx \$3{,}722\). \(1.08^{10} \approx 2.159 \Rightarrow PV \approx 5000/2.159 \approx \$2{,}317\). The higher discount rate reduces PV by about \((3722-2317)/3722 \approx 38\%\) — small changes in the exponent’s base compound into large differences at \(t=10\).

title: Core Course Exercise Bank — Draft
text:
4. Equation of a line

ESM 204
Source: Anna Pede meeting notes — “equation of a line” named directly; grounded in supply/demand curves throughout HW1–HW2.
Exercise 34 (Intro). A demand curve is \(P = 50 - 2Q\). Identify the slope and the y-intercept, and state what each means economically.






NoteSolution





Slope \(= -2\) (price falls $2 for each extra unit demanded); y-intercept \(= 50\) (the “choke price” — the price at which quantity demanded is zero).



Exercise 35 (Medium). A supply curve passes through \((Q=0, P=10)\) and \((Q=100, P=60)\). Find \(P(Q)\) in slope-intercept form.






NoteSolution





Slope \(= (60-10)/(100-0) = 0.5\). \(P = 10 + 0.5Q\).



Exercise 36 (Hard). At a price of $40, quantity demanded is 200 units; at $10, quantity demanded is 350 units. Find the inverse demand equation \(P(Q)\) and the choke price.






NoteSolution





Slope \(= (40-10)/(200-350) = 30/(-150) = -0.2\). Using \((200, 40)\): \(P - 40 = -0.2(Q-200) \Rightarrow P = 80 - 0.2Q\). Choke price (at \(Q=0\)): $80.



Source: real HW1 “Food bank markets” problem — solving Demand = Supply for equilibrium price and quantity. (Moved here from Topic 1: finding a market equilibrium is finding where two lines — demand and supply — intersect, so these fit more naturally alongside single-line exercises than among the single-formula algebra exercises above.)
Exercise 37 (Intro). Demand: \(P = 40 - 2Q\). Supply: \(P = 10 + 3Q\). Solve for the equilibrium quantity and price.






NoteSolution





\(40 - 2Q = 10 + 3Q \Rightarrow 30 = 5Q \Rightarrow Q = 6\). Then \(P = 40 - 2(6) = 28\).



Exercise 38 (Medium). Demand: \(P = 450 - 0.15Q\). Supply: \(P = 10 + 0.1Q\). Solve for equilibrium \(Q\) and \(P\).






NoteSolution





\(450 - 0.15Q = 10 + 0.1Q \Rightarrow 440 = 0.25Q \Rightarrow Q = 1760\). Then \(P = 10 + 0.1(1760) = 186\).



Exercise 39 (Hard). Demand: \(P = 2(300 - 0.5Q)\). Supply: \(P = 50 + Q\). Solve for equilibrium \(Q\) and \(P\).






NoteSolution





Distribute first: \(P = 600 - Q\). Set equal to supply: \(600 - Q = 50 + Q \Rightarrow 550 = 2Q \Rightarrow Q = 275\), \(P = 325\).





ESM 201
Source: instructor note — “equations for lines and hyperbolas” listed among 201’s core algebra needs.
Exercise 40 (Intro). A linear length–weight relationship for a fish species is \(W = 5L - 20\) (grams, cm). What is the weight of a 15 cm fish?






NoteSolution





\(W = 5(15) - 20 = 55\) g.



Exercise 41 (Medium). Two data points relate stream temperature \(T\) (°C) to metabolic rate \(M\): \((T=10, M=20)\) and \((T=20, M=50)\). Find \(M(T)\).






NoteSolution





Slope \(= (50-20)/(20-10) = 3\). \(M = 20 + 3(T-10) = 3T - 10\).



Exercise 42 (Hard). Per-capita growth rate declines linearly with density: at \(N=0\), rate \(=0.3\)/yr; at \(N=K=600\), rate \(=0\). Write the linear equation and find \(N\) where the rate equals \(0.1\)/yr.






NoteSolution





Slope \(= (0-0.3)/(600-0) = -0.0005\). Rate\((N) = 0.3 - 0.0005N\). Set \(=0.1\): \(0.2 = 0.0005N \Rightarrow N = 400\). (This is the logistic per-capita rate \(r(1-N/K)\) in disguise.)





ESM 203
Source: Darcy’s law from the ESM 203 quiz sheet — hydraulic head is linear in distance between wells.
Exercise 43 (Intro). Hydraulic head drops linearly from 80 m to 65 m over a horizontal distance of 500 m. Find the slope \(dh/dL\).






NoteSolution





\((65-80)/500 = -0.03\).



Exercise 44 (Medium). Using \(dh/dL = -0.03\) and hydraulic conductivity \(K = 0.015\) m/day, use Darcy’s law \(q = -K(dh/dL)\) to find the specific discharge.






NoteSolution





\(q = -0.015 \times (-0.03) = 0.00045\) m/day.



Exercise 45 (Hard). Two wells are 400 m apart. Well A has head 120 m; Well B has head 96 m. Write \(h(x)\) as a linear function of distance \(x\) from Well A, and predict the head at \(x=250\) m.






NoteSolution





Slope \(= (96-120)/400 = -0.06\). \(h(x) = 120 - 0.06x\). At \(x=250\): \(h = 120 - 15 = 105\) m.

title: Core Course Exercise Bank — Draft
text:
5. Unit conversion

ESM 202
Source: instructor’s #1 priority — mL↔︎L, and mass/volume concentration units.
Exercise 46 (Intro). Convert 750 mL to liters.






NoteSolution





\(750 \text{ mL} = 0.75\) L.



Exercise 47 (Medium). A stock solution is 4 g/L. Express this in mg/mL.






NoteSolution





\(4 \text{ g/L} = 4000 \text{ mg} / 1000 \text{ mL} = 4\) mg/mL.



Exercise 48 (Hard). A pollutant concentration is 12 μg/mL. Convert this to kg/m³.






NoteSolution





\(1 \text{ mL} = 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3\), so \(12\ \mu\text{g}/10^{-6}\text{ m}^3 = 12\times10^{6}\ \mu\text{g/m}^3\). Convert \(\mu\)g to kg (\(1\ \mu\text{g} = 10^{-9}\) kg): \(12\times10^{6} \times 10^{-9} = 0.012\) kg/m³.





ESM 203
Source: real quiz-prep slide — the lake-area example and area/volume conversions flagged as a struggle point.
Exercise 49 (Intro). Convert an area of 3.2 km² to m².






NoteSolution





\(3.2 \text{ km}^2 \times (1000\text{ m/km})^2 = 3.2\times10^{6}\) m².



Exercise 50 (Medium). A lake has average depth 8 m and surface area 2.5 km². Using Volume = depth × area, find the volume in m³.






NoteSolution





Area \(= 2.5\times10^{6}\) m². Volume \(= 8 \times 2.5\times10^{6} = 2\times10^{7}\) m³.



Exercise 51 (Hard). A watershed receives 45 mm/year of precipitation over an area of 1,800 km². Find the total annual volume of precipitation in m³/year.






NoteSolution





\(45 \text{ mm} = 0.045\) m. Area \(= 1800\times10^{6} = 1.8\times10^{9}\) m². Volume \(= 0.045 \times 1.8\times10^{9} = 8.1\times10^{7}\) m³/year.

title: Core Course Exercise Bank — Draft
text:
6. Reading and interpreting a graph

ESM 204
Source: Anna Pede — reading graphs ranked the #1 most important math tool in the course; grounded in the kinked aggregate demand curve from HW1.
Exercise 52 (Intro). A supply-and-demand graph shows the demand curve hitting the y-axis at \(P=\$60\) and the supply curve hitting it at \(P=\$5\). What does each y-intercept represent?






NoteSolution





Demand y-intercept = the choke price (maximum willingness to pay, at \(Q=0\)). Supply y-intercept = the minimum price needed to induce any positive supply.



Exercise 53 (Medium). An aggregate demand curve has a kink at \((Q=1000, P=\$400)\) (as in the peanut-butter market from HW1). What does the kink tell you about the market, and which price range has more than one buyer group active?






NoteSolution





Above $400, only one demand segment is active; below $400, a second buyer group’s demand adds in, making the aggregate curve flatter (more responsive to price) below the kink.



Exercise 54 (Hard). A graph shows marginal benefit (MB) falling from $1200 to $0 as abatement rises from 0 to 800 tons, and marginal abatement cost (MAC) rising from $70 to $800, crossing MB near \((A{=}320, P{=}\$715)\). A dashed line $70 above MB represents the marginal external benefit (MEB). From the graph alone, how would you locate the socially optimal abatement level, and is it larger or smaller than the market equilibrium?






NoteSolution





The socially optimal level is where MB shifted up by MEB (i.e., MSB) crosses MAC. Since MSB lies above MB everywhere, that crossing happens at a larger abatement quantity than the market equilibrium (MB–MAC crossing).





ESM 203
Source: the saturation vapor pressure curve and water-density-vs-temperature graph used in ESM 203 lecture/quiz materials.
Exercise 55 (Intro). A graph of saturation vapor pressure \(e_s\) (kPa) vs. temperature (°C) starts near 0 at −30°C and reaches about 4.2 kPa at 30°C. Is the relationship linear or nonlinear, and how can you tell from the shape?






NoteSolution





Nonlinear — the curve gets steeper as \(T\) increases rather than rising at a constant rate, unlike a straight line.



Exercise 56 (Medium). On that same graph, a parcel of air has actual vapor pressure 1.0 kPa. Reading across to the curve, it intersects at about \(T=7°C\). What does this temperature represent?






NoteSolution





The dew point temperature — the temperature at which the parcel would be saturated (RH = 100%) at its current actual vapor pressure.



Exercise 57 (Hard). A graph of water density (kg/m³) vs. temperature peaks near 1000 kg/m³ at about 4°C and decreases on both sides. Explain what this implies for how a lake freezes from the surface down rather than the bottom up.






NoteSolution





Water is densest at ~4°C, so 4°C water sinks to the bottom while colder water (and ice), being less dense, stays near the surface. That’s why lakes freeze top-down, insulating the water below and letting aquatic life survive winter.





ESM 201
Source: standard logistic growth curve reading, supporting the instructor’s “beginning calculus” and graph-based intuition for population dynamics.
Exercise 58 (Intro). A graph shows population size \(N(t)\) rising in an S-shape, leveling off at \(N=1000\). What does that horizontal asymptote represent?






NoteSolution





The carrying capacity, \(K\).



Exercise 59 (Medium). On a logistic growth curve, where (approximately) is the population growing fastest, and what fraction of carrying capacity does that typically correspond to?






NoteSolution





At the inflection point, typically \(N = K/2\).



Exercise 60 (Hard). A graph plots per-capita growth rate \(\left(\frac{1}{N}\frac{dN}{dt}\right)\) against population size \(N\), a straight line from \((N=0, \text{rate}=r_{max})\) to \((N=K, \text{rate}=0)\). What do the two intercepts represent, and what does the negative slope mean biologically?






NoteSolution





Y-intercept = maximum per-capita growth rate (density-independent growth at low \(N\)); x-intercept = carrying capacity, where growth rate hits zero. The negative slope reflects negative density dependence: as the population grows, resources become limiting and the per-capita growth rate declines.

title: Core Course Exercise Bank — Draft
text:
7. Derivatives interpretation

ESM 201
Source: instructor note — “if they know dn/dt notation, and that (dn)/(Ndt) = (1/N)(dn/dt), I’ll be thrilled.”
Exercise 61 (Intro). In the notation \(dN/dt\), what does this represent in words, and what does \(dN/dt=0\) mean?






NoteSolution





\(dN/dt\) is the instantaneous rate of change of population size with respect to time. \(dN/dt=0\) means the population is momentarily neither growing nor shrinking.



Exercise 62 (Medium). Explain the difference between \(dN/dt\) and \(\frac{1}{N}\frac{dN}{dt}\). Which is the per-capita growth rate, and why is it more useful for comparing populations of very different sizes?






NoteSolution





\(dN/dt\) is the absolute rate (individuals/time). \(\frac{1}{N}\frac{dN}{dt}\) is the per-capita rate — it normalizes by population size, so populations of 10 and 10,000 can be fairly compared on the same scale.



Exercise 63 (Hard). Population 1 has \(dN/dt = 50\) individuals/year at \(N=500\). Population 2 has \(dN/dt = 50\) individuals/year at \(N=5000\). Compute the per-capita growth rate for each, and say which is growing “faster” in a relative sense.






NoteSolution





Pop 1: \(50/500 = 0.10\)/yr (10%). Pop 2: \(50/5000 = 0.01\)/yr (1%). Despite equal absolute growth, Population 1 is growing far faster in relative (per-capita) terms.





ESM 203
Source: real quiz formula — Darcy’s law, \(q = -K_H(dh/dL)\).
Exercise 64 (Intro). In Darcy’s law, what does \(dh/dL\) represent physically, and why the negative sign?






NoteSolution





\(dh/dL\) is the hydraulic gradient — the rate of change of head with distance. The negative sign ensures flow is directed from high head to low head (down-gradient).



Exercise 65 (Medium). If \(dh/dL = 0\) between two wells, what does that imply about groundwater flow between them?






NoteSolution





No flow (\(q=0\)) — there’s no gradient driving movement.



Exercise 66 (Hard). Head declines steeply near a pumping well and levels off farther away. Explain, using \(dh/dL\), why specific discharge \(q\) is largest close to the well.






NoteSolution





\(q\) is proportional to \(dh/dL\). The gradient (steepness of head decline) is greatest near the pumping well, so \(q\) is largest there and falls off as the gradient flattens with distance.





ESM 204
Source: marginal cost/benefit — the economic meaning of a derivative — appears throughout HW1–HW2.
Exercise 67 (Intro). If total cost is \(TC(Q)\), marginal cost is \(MC(Q) = dTC/dQ\). What does \(MC\) represent in words?






NoteSolution





The additional cost of producing one more (infinitesimal) unit of output at output level \(Q\).



Exercise 68 (Medium). A marginal benefit curve is \(MB(A) = 800 - A\). What does it mean that \(MB\) decreases with \(A\), and what is \(MB\) at \(A=800\)?






NoteSolution





Each additional ton abated brings a smaller benefit (diminishing marginal benefit). At \(A=800\), \(MB=0\) — no further benefit from abating more.



Exercise 69 (Hard). Explain, using the idea of marginal (derivative) comparisons, why ignoring a positive marginal external benefit (MEB) leads a policymaker to choose too little abatement relative to the social optimum.






NoteSolution





Marginal social benefit \(MSB = MB + MEB\) exceeds \(MB\) at every abatement level. The market stops at \(MB=MAC\); the social optimum is where \(MSB=MAC\), which — since \(MSB>MB\) — occurs at a higher \(A\). Ignoring MEB means stopping too early, at a point where the full social marginal benefit still exceeds marginal cost.

title: Core Course Exercise Bank — Draft
text:
8. Derivatives, calculating derivatives

ESM 201
Source: instructor note — “beginning calculus especially derivatives & simple differentiation.”
Exercise 70 (Intro). Find \(dN/dt\) if \(N(t) = 5t^2 + 3t\), using the power rule.






NoteSolution





\(dN/dt = 10t + 3\).



Exercise 71 (Medium). For exponential growth \(N(t) = N_0 e^{rt}\), use the chain rule to show \(dN/dt = rN\).






NoteSolution





\(dN/dt = N_0 \cdot r \cdot e^{rt} = r\left(N_0 e^{rt}\right) = rN\).



Exercise 72 (Hard). For logistic growth, treat \(\frac{dN}{dt} = rN(1-N/K)\) as a function of \(N\). Find \(\frac{d}{dN}\left[rN(1-N/K)\right]\) and evaluate it at \(N=K/2\) and \(N=K\). What does the sign tell you at each point?






NoteSolution





Expand: \(rN - rN^2/K\). Derivative: \(r - 2rN/K\). At \(N=K/2\): \(r - r = 0\) (the inflection point — maximum growth rate). At \(N=K\): \(r - 2r = -r < 0\) (growth rate is decreasing there — a stable equilibrium).





ESM 203
Source: rates of change of head and vapor pressure, extending the Darcy’s law/Tetens-formula material in the ESM 203 quiz.
Exercise 73 (Intro). Hydraulic head is \(h(x) = 100 - 0.04x\). Find \(dh/dx\).






NoteSolution





\(dh/dx = -0.04\).



Exercise 74 (Medium). Near 20°C, saturation vapor pressure is locally approximated by \(e_s(T) \approx 2.34 + 0.17(T-20)\). Find \(de_s/dT\) and interpret it.






NoteSolution





\(de_s/dT = 0.17\) kPa/°C — the approximate rate saturation vapor pressure increases per degree of warming near 20°C.



Exercise 75 (Hard). Using \(e_s(T) = 6.112\,e^{\left(\frac{17.67(T-273.15)}{T-29.65}\right)}\), explain qualitatively (from the shape of the curve, without fully differentiating) why \(de_s/dT\) is larger at high temperatures than low ones, and what this implies for a warming climate.






NoteSolution





\(e_s\) vs. \(T\) is increasing and convex (curves upward), so its slope increases with \(T\) — the same amount of warming produces a bigger jump in saturation vapor pressure at higher baseline temperatures. This is a key reason warmer air holds disproportionately more moisture, intensifying precipitation potential as the climate warms.





ESM 204
Source: power/chain rule applied to demand and cost functions throughout HW1–HW2.
Exercise 76 (Intro). Given inverse demand \(P(Q) = 100 - 4Q\), find \(dP/dQ\).






NoteSolution





\(dP/dQ = -4\).



Exercise 77 (Medium). Total abatement cost is \(TAC(A) = 70A + A^2\). Find \(MAC(A) = dTAC/dA\) and evaluate at \(A=50\).






NoteSolution





\(MAC(A) = 70 + 2A\). At \(A=50\): \(MAC = 170\).



Exercise 78 (Hard). A firm’s profit is \(\pi(Q) = 40Q - 0.5Q^2 - 200\). Find the profit-maximizing \(Q^*\) using \(d\pi/dQ=0\), and confirm it’s a maximum with the second derivative.






NoteSolution





\(d\pi/dQ = 40 - Q = 0 \Rightarrow Q^* = 40\). Second derivative: \(d^2\pi/dQ^2 = -1 < 0\), confirming a maximum. \(\pi(40) = 1600 - 800 - 200 = 600\).

title: Core Course Exercise Bank — Draft
text:
9. Integrals interpretation

ESM 204
Source: Anna Pede — “find integral = area under graph (surplus)”; real HW2 marginal-external-benefit example.
Exercise 79 (Intro). Marginal external benefit (MEB) is constant at $70/ton. What does \(\int_0^A MEB\,dA\) represent, and why is it just \(MEB \times A\) here?






NoteSolution





It’s the total external benefit from abating \(A\) tons. Since MEB is constant, the area under the curve is a rectangle (height × width), so total benefit \(= MEB \times A\) — no integration technique needed for a constant function.



Exercise 80 (Medium). A marginal benefit curve is \(MB(A) = 1200 - 1.5A\). What does the total benefit of abating from 0 to 300 tons represent geometrically?






NoteSolution





The area under the \(MB\) line between \(A=0\) and \(A=300\) — since \(MB\) is linear and positive there, that area is a trapezoid (or a rectangle plus a triangle).



Exercise 81 (Hard). Explain why deadweight loss (DWL) from an uncorrected externality is the triangular area between the marginal social benefit (MSB) curve and the MAC curve, between the market quantity and the social optimum — and why this is fundamentally an integral.






NoteSolution





Between the market quantity and the social optimum, \(MSB(A) > MAC(A)\) at every point — each “missed” unit would have added net value. Summing (integrating) that gap \(MSB(A)-MAC(A)\) over the missed range gives total forgone benefit; because both curves are lines, that integral’s shape is a triangle, i.e., the DWL.





ESM 201
Source: natural extension of the dN/dt material — cumulative population change as area under a rate curve.
Exercise 82 (Intro). A population grows at a roughly constant \(dN/dt = 40\) individuals/year for 5 years. What does \(\int_0^5 \frac{dN}{dt}\,dt\) represent, and what’s its value?






NoteSolution





The total change in population size over the 5 years — the area under the constant-rate line — \(= 40 \times 5 = 200\) individuals.



Exercise 83 (Medium). A recruitment rate declines linearly from 100/year to 20/year over 4 years. Find total recruitment over the 4 years using the area under this line.






NoteSolution





Trapezoid area: \(\frac{100+20}{2} \times 4 = 240\) individuals recruited.



Exercise 84 (Hard). A population’s birth rate rises linearly from 20/year to 80/year over 6 years, while a constant harvest of 30 individuals/year is removed throughout. Using areas under curves for each rate, find the net change in population over the 6 years.






NoteSolution





Births (trapezoid area): \(\frac{20+80}{2} \times 6 = 300\) individuals. Harvest (rectangle area): \(30 \times 6 = 180\) individuals. Net change \(= 300 - 180 = 120\) individuals.

title: Core Course Exercise Bank — Draft
text:
10. Integrals, calculating an integral

ESM 204
Source: real HW2 progression — marginal benefit → total benefit / consumer surplus via the power rule; real HW2 total-abatement-cost calculation.
Exercise 85 (Intro). Given \(MB(A) = 1200 - 1.5A\), find \(TB(A) = \int MB(A)\,dA\) (with \(TB(0)=0\)), and evaluate at \(A=300\).






NoteSolution





\(TB(A) = 1200A - 0.75A^2\). \(TB(300) = 1200(300) - 0.75(300)^2 = 360{,}000 - 67{,}500 = 292{,}500\).



Exercise 86 (Medium). Demand is \(P(Q) = 500 - 0.1Q\). At \(Q^*=3000\), the equilibrium price is \(P^*=200\). Find consumer surplus by integrating \(P(Q)\) from 0 to \(Q^*\) and subtracting total expenditure \(P^*Q^*\).






NoteSolution





\(\int_0^{3000}(500-0.1Q)\,dQ = \left[500Q - 0.05Q^2\right]_0^{3000} = 1{,}500{,}000 - 450{,}000 = 1{,}050{,}000\). \(CS = 1{,}050{,}000 - (200\times3000) = 1{,}050{,}000 - 600{,}000 = 450{,}000\). (Check: this matches the triangle formula \(\tfrac12 \times 3000 \times (500-200) = 450{,}000\).)



Exercise 87 (Hard). \(MAC(A) = 70 + 2A\). Find \(TAC(A)\) by integrating, then compute the total cost of abating from 0 to 342.86 tons — and check it against the trapezoid-area method.






NoteSolution





\(TAC(A) = 70A + A^2\). At \(A=342.86\): \(TAC \approx 70(342.86) + 342.86^2 \approx 24{,}000 + 117{,}551 \approx 141{,}551\).
Check via trapezoid: \(MAC(0)=70\), \(MAC(342.86) = 70+2(342.86) \approx 755.7\). Area \(= \frac{70+755.7}{2}\times342.86 \approx 141{,}551\) — matches.





ESM 201
Source: extends the dN/dt power-rule material to recover N(t) or cumulative recruitment from a rate function.
Exercise 88 (Intro). \(dN/dt = 6t\). Find \(N(t)\) given \(N(0)=50\).






NoteSolution





\(N(t) = 3t^2 + C\). \(N(0)=50 \Rightarrow C=50\). \(N(t) = 3t^2 + 50\).



Exercise 89 (Medium). Recruitment rate is \(R(t) = 100 - 5t\) individuals/year (for \(0 \le t \le 20\)). Find total recruitment between \(t=0\) and \(t=10\).






NoteSolution





\(\int_0^{10}(100-5t)\,dt = \left[100t - 2.5t^2\right]_0^{10} = 1000 - 250 = 750\) individuals.



Exercise 90 (Hard). A population’s net rate of change is \(dN/dt = 8t - 15\) individuals/year (growth accelerating over time, offset by a constant harvest of 15/year). Find \(N(t)\) given \(N(0)=100\), and compute \(N(5)\).






NoteSolution





\(N(t) = 4t^2 - 15t + C\). \(N(0)=100 \Rightarrow C=100\). \(N(t) = 4t^2 - 15t + 100\). \(N(5) = 4(25) - 75 + 100 = 100-75+100=125\) individuals.

11. Differential equations example

ESM 201
Source: instructor note — Lotka-Volterra and logistic growth are the flagship applications for ESM 201.
Exercise 91 (Intro). Write the logistic growth equation \(\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(1-\frac{N}{K}\right)\) and explain what each term represents (don’t solve it).






NoteSolution





\(dN/dt\): rate of population change over time. \(r\): intrinsic (maximum per-capita) growth rate. \(N\): current population size. \(K\): carrying capacity. \((1-N/K)\): shrinks toward zero as \(N\) approaches \(K\), representing resource limitation.



Exercise 92 (Medium). With \(r=0.5\)/yr and \(K=1000\), evaluate \(dN/dt\) at \(N=200\) and at \(N=900\). Why is growth faster at \(N=200\)?






NoteSolution





At \(N=200\): \(0.5 \times 200 \times (1-0.2) = 100 \times 0.8 = 80\)/yr. At \(N=900\): \(0.5 \times 900 \times (1-0.9) = 450 \times 0.1 = 45\)/yr. Growth is faster at \(N=200\) because it’s farther from carrying capacity, so the limiting term \((1-N/K)\) is closer to 1.



Exercise 93 (Hard). The Lotka-Volterra equations are \(\frac{dN}{dt} = aN - bNP\) (prey) and \(\frac{dP}{dt} = cbNP - dP\) (predator). What happens to \(dN/dt\) if \(P=0\), and what does this reveal about \(dP/dt\) at the same moment? What does this say about how the two equations are coupled?






NoteSolution





If \(P=0\): \(dN/dt = aN\) (pure exponential prey growth — no predation loss). At the same moment, \(dP/dt = cbN(0) - d(0) = 0\): the predator population can’t grow from zero, since there are no prey-predator encounters to fuel reproduction. The two populations are coupled entirely through the interaction term \(bNP\), which vanishes whenever either population is zero.





ESM 204
Source: instructor note — “the simplest of differential equations” is used in 204, in the context of renewable-resource dynamics.
Exercise 94 (Intro). A resource stock evolves as \(\frac{dS}{dt} = gS - H\), where \(g\) is a growth rate and \(H\) a constant harvest rate. What condition on \(dS/dt\) defines a “sustainable” harvest?






NoteSolution





Sustainability means \(dS/dt = 0\), i.e., \(H = gS\): the harvest exactly matches natural growth at the current stock size, so the stock is stable over time.



Exercise 95 (Medium). With \(g=0.1\)/year and current stock \(S=2000\) tons, what harvest rate \(H\) makes this a steady state?






NoteSolution





\(H = gS = 0.1 \times 2000 = 200\) tons/year.



Exercise 96 (Hard). Suppose \(\frac{dS}{dt} = gS - H\) with \(g=0.08\)/year, but the harvest \(H\) is fixed at 250 tons/year regardless of stock size (rather than adjusted proportionally). Find the stock level \(S^*\) at which this fixed harvest is exactly sustainable, and explain what happens to \(dS/dt\) if \(S\) drifts above or below \(S^*\).






NoteSolution





Steady state: \(gS^* = H \Rightarrow S^* = H/g = 250/0.08 = 3125\) tons. If \(S > S^*\): \(gS > H\), so \(dS/dt > 0\) — the stock keeps growing, unboundedly in this simple model. If \(S < S^*\): \(gS < H\), so \(dS/dt < 0\) — the stock keeps shrinking toward zero. Unlike a harvest set proportional to stock size, a fixed-quantity harvest makes \(S^*\) an unstable equilibrium rather than a stable one.

Follow order of operations (a.k.a. PEDMAS)
Never change an equation. Instead, rewrite them into more useful forms

 Always add/substract/multiply/divide by the same number on both sides. More generally, always apply the same function to both sides of the equation.

Exponents make algebra more interesting!

Example
The expression \(x^3\) means \(x\) multiplied by itself 3 times: \[x^3=x * x * x\]

More generally, \[x^n = x \text{ to the power of } n.\]


Intuitively, the exponent \(n\) tells us how many times to multiply the basis \(x\) by itself:
\[x^n = \underbrace{x \times x \times \ldots \times x}_{n \text{ times}}\]
But the exponent can be any (real) number, not only integers!

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
What are exponents good for?



They can describe really big numbers

Diameter of the Milky Way = 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 meters = \[10^{21} \text{ m}\]

And also really small numbers

Diameter of a human red blood cell = 0.0000000001 meters = \[10^{-10} \text{ m}\]

This way, we can use exponents to describe exponential growth and decay. Many environmental variables behave in this way.

title: Bren Math Workshop
text:
Roots of polynomials

A zero, root, or solution for a polynomial is a value of \(x\) that makes the polynomial equal to zero.

Fundamental Theorem of Algebra

A polynomial \[
a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+...+a_1x+a_0
\]
of degree \(n\) has exactly \(n\) roots \(r_1, \ldots, r_n\) and it can be refactored as
\[
c(x-r_1) ... (x-r_n).
\]

The numbers \(c\) and \(r_1, \ldots, r_n\) may be complex!

Example:
Consider the function \(x - 2\), this is just a 1st degree polynomial. It has a single root, \(r_1=2\).

Solve \(x^2-x-12=0\), where \(a=1\), \(b=-1\), \(c=-12\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a} \\

&= \frac{1\pm\sqrt{49}}{2} \\
&= \frac{1\pm7}{2}
\end{aligned}

1) Expand the following expressions:
